projects.name: Vestige Engine
projects.tagline: A 3D game engine built from scratch.
projects.blurb: A 3D engine written in C++ from the ground up, for walking through spaces you build yourself. Realistic lighting and shadows, volumetric fog, a meadow of a million grass blades, physics and character animation. It comes with a built-in editor and profiling tools.

screenshots.alt: A first-person view across a meadow of tall, bright green grass, with a small pond, scattered pine trees and a hazy lilac evening sky.

The Vestige editor, with a list of scene objects on the left, a grassy meadow with pine trees in the centre view where a selected object shows red, green and blue move arrows, and that object's position, rotation and scale on the right.
The Vestige editor showing a material test scene: blocks of red brick, dark wood and pale stone standing on a pale floor marked with a placement grid, with tufts of grass between them.

The Vestige editor with its Settings window open on the Accessibility tab, over the meadow scene. A sidebar lists the Display, Audio, Controls, Gameplay, Accessibility and Language tabs. The Accessibility tab has a UI scale of 1.0x, checkboxes for high contrast and reduced motion (both off) and subtitles (on), a subtitle size of medium and a colour-vision filter set to none. Below, under 'Post-process accessibility', switches for depth of field and motion blur each note '(effect not yet shipped — preference is saved)', and a fog switch is on.

video.caption: A 67-second trailer for Vestige, with quiet background music and soft clicks but no speech; everything it says is written on screen. White and violet lettering sits over a dark background with soft coloured glows. It opens with "Explore places on foot. Build them in one editor." The first clip, captioned "A meadow of a million grass blades", glides over tall grass toward a small pond under a pale sky. Then the Vestige logo, an arched doorway filled with golden light, and "A free 3D engine for walkable worlds". Clips of the engine follow, each with a caption below. "Press Esc: walk, then edit": the view switches between walking in the grass and the editor, with its panels around the scene. "Place it, move it, undo it": a white cube is placed in the grass and moved, then the move is undone. "Type exact values to move, turn and stretch": numbers are typed into the panel on the right, and the cube turns and stretches. "Change any material's colour": the cube turns pink, then red. "Recolour the sun and relight the whole scene": the sunlight's colour is changed, and the whole meadow turns a dusky purple, then golden, then a deep sunset red. "Walk it yourself": a walk through the grass to the pond, where lily pads float on green water. "Light, haze and reflections, drawn live": the pond from further back, with haze over the distant grass. "Graphics settings, changed live": the quality setting is changed in a settings menu. "A colour-vision filter built in": a filter is chosen from a menu, and the colours of the grass shift. Three lines follow: "Realistic light, fog and shadows", "Quality presets for older graphics cards" and "Remappable keys, reduced motion". Then "Linux · Windows" and "Download it and start walking". It ends on the logo with "Free and fully open source", "Download it free at antsprojectshub.co.za", and links to support the project on GitHub Sponsors, Patreon and Paybru.

projects.name: Ants Terminal
projects.tagline: A fast, modern terminal for Linux that makes Claude Code cheaper and easier to use.
projects.blurb: A terminal is the window where you type commands to your computer. This is a fast, good-looking one for Linux, built from scratch. Its party trick is working hand in hand with Claude Code, Anthropic's AI coding assistant: it answers many of Claude's everyday questions itself and hands back a short summary instead of a wall of text, so you spend less. Its tools run on your own computer and send nothing anywhere.

screenshots.alt: Ants Terminal running a live Claude Code session over a dark theme, with a row of per-project tabs and an assistant working through a task

The Roadmap window on its Next tab: each section of the project's plan sits on one line, with its release number, title, kind and target date in tidy columns, and one section opened to show its sub-sections
The Review Changes dialog showing a project's git status and unpushed commits, with Refresh and Copy Diff buttons
Ants Terminal in a different colour theme, displaying a detailed multi-thread stack trace from a crash report

video.caption: A 32-second trailer for Ants Terminal, with background music and soft clicks but no speech; everything it says is written on screen. It is styled like a computer terminal: green and white monospaced lettering over a dark background of faint scrolling text. It opens with "Your terminal looks dated. Plain text, one window.", then the Ants Terminal logo, a pale blue ant, and "A fast, good-looking terminal for Linux". Two clips of the app follow, each with a caption below. "Colour and symbols, crisp and clear": a build command runs in a project called stargazer, printing green ticks beside each compile and link step, 42 tests passed, and "Done in 0.8s" followed by a sparkle, a lambda, a star and a moon. "Switch themes in one click": with the same output on screen, the colour theme is changed from the menu and the whole window recolours, from a purple-grey look to a darker one with orange file names. Three lines follow: "Eleven built-in colour themes", "Split panes, side by side" and "Built for Claude Code". It ends on the logo with "Free and fully open source", "Download it free at antsprojectshub.co.za", and links to support the project on GitHub Sponsors, Patreon and Paybru.

projects.name: RetroDB
projects.tagline: A ROM library manager for 140+ retro gaming systems.
projects.blurb: A web-based collection manager for retro games across 140+ platforms: hybrid metadata scraping, one-click emulator launch, achievements and trophy integration, ROM tools (CHD conversion, duplicate finding, multi-disc handling), an analytics dashboard, multiple themes and languages, and role-based multi-user access.

screenshots.alt: The RetroDB library page in its dark neon theme, filled with invented games: a sidebar menu on the left, a big glowing "All Games" heading reading "39 games across all systems", a search box with system and type dropdowns, filter buttons for genre, series, publisher, developer, players, perspective, dimension, rating, source, achievements and bonus discs, an A-to-Z jump bar, and the first game card, "Aqua Rampart" for the Sega Mega Drive, showing its red cover art, genre, developer, publisher, year, age-rating badges, an "In Progress" status and two review scores.

One game's page, "Paper Planet" for the Sony PlayStation, with a blurred moonlit backdrop behind a row of Play, Clear, Edit, Scrape and Delete buttons, a blue cover picture, tags for the year 1997, 4 players, the Europe region and two scores, a play-status dropdown set to "Not Started", a one-line description, the publisher, developer and genre, Teen and PEGI 12 age-rating badges, and a strip of three pixel-art gameplay screenshots underneath.

The "Gaming Systems" page with a "5 consoles detected" badge, a search box and type and feature filters, and a grid of console cards: the Nintendo 64 and Game Boy Advance in full view with their logos, 7 games each, a console or handheld tag and a RetroAchievements tag, and the Sega Mega Drive and PlayStation cards starting below.

The dashboard, with tabs for Overview, Systems, Playing, Added and Status, "Random Game" and "Scan Library" buttons, a "Collection Health" panel showing 100% overall, with smaller rings at 100% for box art and descriptions and 0% for achievements, and summary tiles for 5 systems, 39 games, 0 missing metadata and 39 complete.

video.caption: A 52-second trailer for RetroDB, with background music and soft clicks but no speech; everything it says is written on screen. It is styled like an arcade game: pixel lettering over a dark purple sky, with a neon grid floor and a striped setting sun. It opens with "Thousands of retro games. Just filenames in folders.", then the RetroDB logo and "Your retro library, beautifully organised". Clips of the app follow, each with a caption below. "Pick a system, see every game": a Gaming Systems page shows cards for the Game Boy Advance, Nintendo 64, NES, Mega Drive, PlayStation and Super Nintendo. Nintendo 64 is clicked, and its games appear with their box art, among them GoldenEye 007, Super Mario 64 and The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time. "Nine age-rating systems": the view zooms in on GoldenEye 007's row of age-rating badges from different countries. "Covers, videos, screenshots and ratings": Chrono Trigger's page shows its cover, a story summary, rating badges, screenshots and a video, then a moving scene from the game fills the frame. "Five game databases, searched at once": "Super Metroid" is searched in a Search Metadata window, and results come back in five columns, one each for ES-DE, ScreenScraper, RAWG, TheGamesDB and IGDB. "Seven themes, one click each": theme cards on the settings page are clicked one after another, and the whole app changes colour each time. "Speaks 21 languages": the language list is opened, and the app switches to Japanese. It ends on the logo with "Free and fully open source", "Download it free at antsprojectshub.co.za", and links to support the project on GitHub Sponsors, Patreon and Paybru.

projects.name: MAME Curator
projects.tagline: Picks the best playable arcade games from a MAME set.
projects.blurb: Turns a 40,000-machine MAME set into a human-sized arcade library. It intelligently chooses the best version of each game, lets you override picks in a browser UI, copies the chosen ROMs plus required BIOSes, and writes a ready-to-use RetroArch playlist.

screenshots.alt: The MAME Curator library in a dark theme, filtered to the Capcom Classics collection: a grid of arcade cover art for 1941, 1942, 1943, Armored Warriors, Avengers and more, with search and filter controls in a left sidebar. Across the top, five featured collection tiles give their sizes: Capcom Classics 121 games, Beat 'em Ups 85, Run & Gun Shooters 83, Best of 1992 303, and SHMUPS — Vertical 260.

The Alternative versions panel open beside the library for Street Fighter II: The World Warrior. It says there are 38 versions, gives a short summary of the game from Wikipedia, and lists each version with a red Use this version button.

The Dry-run preview window over the library, after five Street Fighter games were added to the list. It reports 5 new files to copy, 0 to replace, 0 to skip and 0 BIOS files, with Cancel and Copy buttons.

The Copy in progress window over the library, part-way through copying four Street Fighter games. It reads 3 / 4 — sfiii2n and State: Copying, with the red progress bar about three-quarters full and Pause and Cancel buttons.

The Settings page on its Filters tab: switches that drop BIOS and device machines, Japanese-only games, games with preliminary emulation, games needing CHD disk images, and mature content, all switched on, plus fields to drop games by year, category, genre, publisher and developer.

video.caption: A silent 44-second tour of MAME Curator in its browser interface; a white circle marks the pointer. It opens on the full game library, then clicks the Capcom Classics collection: after a moment's loading the grid fills with Capcom cover art. Street fighter ii is typed into the search box and the grid narrows to Street Fighter games. Clicking Street Fighter II opens the Alternative versions panel, listing its versions with a short Wikipedia summary; Use this version is clicked on one release and the panel closes. Four games are added to the list one after another and the counter at the bottom climbs to 4. Dry-run opens a preview of the files to copy, and Copy is pressed inside it. A Copy in progress window counts up from 1 of 4 to 4 of 4 as each game is copied, then closes, and the list at the bottom is empty again.

projects.name: Perch
projects.tagline: Remembers every window's size and spot, with snap layouts.
projects.blurb: A system-tray app that remembers where each window lives — position, size, monitor and virtual desktop — and restores it on reopen. Snap presets, named layouts, per-monitor profiles, a rules engine and global hotkeys, with backends for X11 and KWin/Wayland.

screenshots.alt: Perch's right-click tray menu. Its greyed-out first line shows the active profile and layout, "Perch — docked / coding". Below are Layouts, Snap focused window, a Pause Perch checkbox, Reapply rules now, Configure Perch, Open config folder, Donate, Report an issue, About Perch and Quit Perch. The Snap focused window submenu is open beside it, listing Maximize on this monitor, left and right halves, the four quarters, Centre (keep size), Centre (60%) and a custom preset called "Reading column".

Perch's settings window on its Layouts page. A layout named "coding" is selected, described as "Editor left, browser right", and has two entries: the code editor takes 60% of the primary screen's width on the left, and Firefox the remaining 40% on the right.

Perch's Rules page, noting that rules are checked from top to bottom, the first match wins, and a row can be dragged to change the order. A table lists five example rules, each with the window it matches and where it goes: the browser fills the big screen, the terminal goes on the left, chat goes on the laptop screen, the editor takes a set size when docked, and small settings dialogs are centred.

Perch's General settings page. Checkboxes to start Perch at login and to restore each window's remembered position when it reopens are ticked; showing a notification on restore is not. Below are a theme choice, set to light, and a button to run the setup wizard again. A sidebar on the left lists the other pages: Windows, Rules, Layouts, Profiles, Hotkeys, Exclusions and Import / Export.

video.caption: A silent 31-second tour of Perch, using made-up windows and settings. It opens on Perch's tray menu, listing Layouts, Snap focused window, Pause Perch, Reapply rules now, Configure Perch and more. The Preferences window then opens on its General page. The Windows page lists the open windows Perch is tracking, with each one's app, title, screen, size and position. A new "Team chat" window appears in the list, then moves to the right half of the laptop screen, and its row updates to the new position. The Rules page shows five rules, such as "Browser fills the big screen" and "Terminal on the left", each with the window it matches and where that window goes. The Layouts page shows a "coding" layout that puts the editor on the left and the terminal on the right. The Profiles page shows a "docked" profile tied to a two-screen setup. The Hotkeys page shows keyboard shortcuts for two saved window positions. The video then fades to black.

projects.name: RetroArch
projects.tagline: My fork of the reference frontend for 100+ emulator cores.
projects.blurb: RetroArch is the de-facto frontend for the libretro API, supporting 100+ emulator and game-engine cores across a huge range of platforms. This is my personal fork tracking the upstream libretro/RetroArch project with my own changes on top.

screenshots.alt: RetroArch's Ozone menu in dark grey. A sidebar on the left lists Main Menu, Settings, History, Favorites, Images, Import Content, Contentless Cores and Explore. The main panel lists Load Core (highlighted), Load Content, Playlists, Netplay, Online Updater, Information and Configuration File, each with a one-line description underneath.

RetroArch's XMB menu: a row of category icons runs across a flowing blue wave background, in the style of a games-console home screen. Below it is a vertical list starting with Load Core, then Load Content, Playlists, Netplay, Online Updater, Information, Configuration File, Show Desktop Menu, Restart and Quit.

RetroArch's RGUI menu, a retro text-only style: green and white pixel lettering on a dark checkered background inside a green border. It lists the main menu options with an arrow pointing at Load Core, and "Select which core to use." along the bottom.

projects.name: Hell's Gate
projects.tagline: Dante's Inferno, rebuilt to run natively on PC, now buildable on openSUSE.
projects.blurb: Hell's Gate turns the Xbox 360 game Dante's Inferno into a native Windows and Linux program, with no emulator. We added openSUSE Tumbleweed build support, and the author merged it into the main project.

projects.name: Album Builder
projects.tagline: Curate albums from recordings, with lyric-sync and reports.
projects.blurb: A desktop tool for shaping albums out of a folder of recordings: per-track curation, drag-to-reorder, live preview with optional lyric syncing, cross-album reuse tracking, a built-in music player, and export to M3U playlists, numbered folders (Linux) and polished PDF/HTML reports.

screenshots.alt: Album Builder's main screen in a dark theme, with an invented library: a song library list on the left with the song "Lanterns on the Water" highlighted, the track order for a draft album called "Night Drive" in the middle, and on the right the song now playing with its colourful fractal cover art, title, album and artist, above playback controls.

Album Builder's Player tab in a dark theme, with an invented library. On the left, a searchable library lists ten songs by title and artist. In the middle is the song "Paper Boats" by Harbour Lights, with its colourful fractal cover art above the title, and playback controls, a time readout and a volume slider along the bottom. On the right is a lyrics panel, and below it Up Next and Playlists tabs, with Up Next showing "Nothing queued".

The same Player tab with the app in Arabic. The whole window is mirrored right to left: the menus, tabs and headings are in Arabic, the library sits on the right, and the lyrics panel and Up Next are on the left. The song titles stay in English, and the play controls keep their usual left-to-right order.
Adding a song whose name you already have: a message says one song was added, both copies are kept, and the new copy was saved as "02 - Slow Tide (2).mp3".

projects.name: Snatch
projects.tagline: A friendly desktop frontend for yt-dlp.
projects.blurb: A graphical front-end for yt-dlp with four tabs: download (paste or drag a URL, queue many), search (with preview), media info (inspect local files), and history. Cookie import for age-gated videos, SponsorBlock, subtitles, audio merging and one-click self-update.

screenshots.alt: Snatch's Download tab with Big Buck Bunny loaded (© Blender Foundation, CC-BY 3.0): a thumbnail of the giant rabbit beside its title and running time, and below it a table of the 47 available formats, listing audio-only and video streams by type, resolution, size and codec, with buttons to pick the best video, the best MP4 or audio only.

The Search tab after searching Blender Studio's own channel for "open movie": a numbered list of results such as Spring, CHARGE and Coffee Run, each with its channel, running time and view count, above a built-in video player area.

The History tab listing four past downloads, Big Buck Bunny, Sintel, Elephants Dream and Tears of Steel, with the date, the format such as MP4 1080p or MP3 audio, and where each file was saved, plus buttons to open the file or its folder.

projects.name: Games Hub
projects.tagline: Fourteen desktop games in one small window.
projects.blurb: Chess, Draughts, Reversi, Minesweeper, Sudoku, Snake, 2048, Pinball, Hearts, Canasta and four kinds of patience — Klondike, Spider, FreeCell and Pyramid — in a single Qt 6 window sized to sit beside whatever you are actually working on. The board games play against the computer at three strengths. Nothing to install: each download carries its own copy of Qt, so it runs on a machine that has never had it.

screenshots.alt: The Games Hub start screen, headed "Pick a game", showing large dark tiles in rows of three, each with a picture and a name: Chess, Reversi, Draughts, Minesweeper, Solitaire, Spider, FreeCell, Pyramid and Sudoku, with more below.
A new game of Klondike solitaire on a green table, with the draw pile top left, four empty ace spaces top right, and seven columns of large, clearly printed cards below.
A chess board at the start of a game, cream and green squares with the pieces in their starting positions, labelled a to h and 1 to 8, with Easy, Medium and Hard difficulty buttons in the toolbar.

A four-player Canasta game in progress on a deep red table, with the player's hand of large cards at the bottom, both teams' melds laid out in the middle, the stock and discard pile in the centre, and the two team scores in the top corners.

projects.name: DOOM Ants
projects.tagline: A ray-traced reimagining of id's DOOM on modern Linux.
projects.blurb: A two-stage modernisation of the 1997 DOOM source: first bringing the ancient code to SDL2 on 64-bit Linux, then evolving the renderer toward true 3D with hardware ray tracing, dynamic lighting and volumetric effects — while keeping the original's feel. Early days.

screenshots.alt: The classic DOOM title screen with the New Game menu, rendered by DOOM Ants
Classic DOOM gameplay in a widescreen view — a marine facing a computer-room level over a blue floor
Classic mode's Video menu, now drawn in the same sharp style as Solid and Ultra, over a dimmed game view
The same DOOM level with hardware ray tracing — realistic shadows and dynamic lighting darkening the room

projects.name: UT Ants
projects.tagline: Plays your Unreal Tournament maps on a modern engine.
projects.blurb: Unreal Tournament is from 1999 and people are still playing it and still making maps for it — one Monster Hunt server here carries 515 of them. The engine underneath is frozen: shadows are painted into the walls at build time, and the computer players walk into a closed door and stop. UT Ants is a new engine that reads the maps you already have and rebuilds each one as a modernised version of itself — moving shadows, real materials, fog and light shafts — while running, dodging and shock-combos feel exactly as your hands expect. It ships none of Epic's content: you bring your own copy of the game. Very early, and there is nothing to download yet.

screenshots.alt: Arcane Temple's upper hall, before and after. Left: the far end of the hall is lit but the near walls and ceiling are almost black. Right: the same view with an added torch on the right-hand wall, lighting the stonework and ceiling around it.
Arcane Temple's pillared passage, before and after. Left: dim stone pillars with no light between them. Right: the same spot with an added torch burning on a stone block between two pillars.

projects.name: Slipcase
projects.tagline: Turns flat 2D game covers into realistic 3D box renders.
projects.blurb: A desktop tool that turns a flat 2D cover image into a photorealistic 3D box render — front, spine, top edge and a soft shadow, at the real millimetre measurements of fifteen case types from NES cartridge boxes to Switch cases. It can find the artwork for you, invent a spine when your cover has none, do a whole folder at once, and save an animation of the box turning to an angle and back. Output is transparent PNG sized for RetroArch or LaunchBox. It comes as a single download for Linux, Windows or Mac.

screenshots.alt: Before and after: a flat, made-up game cover on the left, and the same cover rendered by Slipcase as a 3D DVD case on the right.
Slipcase's main window: a flat game cover loaded on the left, and its rendered 3D box with spine and reflection in the preview on the right.

projects.name: Contact List

projects.blurb: A desktop contact manager for people and companies: search, custom fields, and two-way sync with Google Contacts, built with a security-first design.

projects.name: Rolodex
projects.tagline: An encrypted credential vault with auto-masking.
projects.blurb: A GTK4 password manager that keeps your logins in one encrypted file (Fernet + PBKDF2), masks sensitive fields automatically, and shows live two-factor codes.

screenshots.alt: Rolodex's main window, holding an invented vault. A sidebar groups entries under Email, Games, Shopping and Work. On the right, a Fastmail entry shows its email address, a hidden password, and a live six-digit two-factor code with a countdown ring.
The Password Health check, which lists every stored password from weakest to strongest, marks those reused across accounts, and sums them up as 4 weak or fair and 2 reused.
The Edit Entry window. Each field has a label, a value, a Hide switch for secrets, a button to generate a new password, and a drag handle for reordering.

It opens on an entry called Fastmail, showing an email address, a hidden password, a hidden two-factor setup key, a six-digit sign-in code with a countdown ring, and a web address, each with a coloured stripe and an icon for its type. projects.name: Rusty PSN
projects.tagline: Download PS3 & PS4 game updates straight from Sony.
projects.blurb: A Rust tool that fetches PS3 and PS4 game updates directly from Sony's servers, with both a graphical app and a command-line interface. My fork of RainbowCookie32's rusty-psn.

Two PS3 games in the list, LittleBigPlanet and Uncharted 2, with Uncharted 2 marked as downloading; the bar along the bottom shows one active download at 30 percent, its speed and the time left

The RPCS3 Library window over the update list: three installed PS3 games, with Uncharted 2 marked Up to date at version 01.09, LittleBigPlanet marked Update available from 01.18 to 01.30, and an Update All Outdated button

projects.name: finbreak
projects.tagline: Breaks your finances into categories — private and offline.
projects.blurb: A private, offline desktop app that reads the statements your bank already gives you (CSV, OFX or PDF) and breaks your finances down into categories across multiple accounts, with charts, a balance forecast, automatic transfer and recurring-payment detection, and password-protected PDF reports. Your data never leaves your machine.

video.caption: A silent 32-second tour of finbreak, in dark theme, using invented demo data. It opens on the lock screen, where the master password is typed. The Home dashboard follows for August — 'August looked like a normal month', net R 10,533.21 — where three donut charts break down spending by category, income by source and transfers between accounts. It then moves through Transactions (306 rows sorted into categories such as Groceries, Fuel and Dining out), the Categories tree, Recurring (suggested payments above confirmed ones), Accounts and Transfers, before returning to the dashboard. Recorded with demoreel.

screenshots.alt: The finbreak home dashboard in dark theme, with 'Previous month' selected. A one-line summary reads "August looked like a normal month." above a net of R 10,533.21, with an Alerts button and an account picker at the top right. Three donut charts break down spending by category, income (Salary, Interest) and transfers (Cheque account to Savings). Below them, panels list Spending R 21,551.79 (Rent/Mortgage R 9,500, Groceries R 3,524.50, Transport R 3,012.45 and more), Income R 32,085.00 and Transfers R 3,000.00.

The Transactions view in light theme: a search box, a date-range filter and account and category pickers above a sortable table of 306 transactions with Date, Amount, Currency, Description, Account and Category columns. Rows show South African merchants such as Shell, Pick n Pay, Ocean Basket, Bolt, KFC and Checkers sorted into categories like Fuel, Groceries, Dining out and Ride-hailing, alongside a salary, interest and transfers to savings.

The Categories screen in dark theme showing the category tree. Expenditure branches into Bills & utilities (Electricity, Internet, Mobile), Entertainment (Dining out, Streaming), Transport (Fuel, Ride-hailing), Groceries, Insurance, Medical, Rent/Mortgage and more; Income branches into Gifts, Interest, Lottery, Salary, Sales and Other income. The Recurring view in light theme with two tables. 'Suggested recurring items' lists payments finbreak has detected — Outsurance, an FNB credit, Dis-Chem and City of Cape Town — each with direction, monthly cadence, amount, next due date and times seen, awaiting Confirm or Dismiss. projects.name: OneUp
projects.tagline: One-click openSUSE updates from a single window.
projects.blurb: A no-nonsense update dashboard for openSUSE (Tumbleweed and Leap) that runs the five updates you actually need — system packages, Flatpaks, firmware, leftover-package cleanup and cache cleanup — the correct way, from one window. Each task is a toggle. Check for updates read-only, roll back to a pre-update snapshot in one click, and let it check or even update weekly in the background. It never runs as root — privileged work goes through your desktop's standard password prompt.

screenshots.alt: The OneUp window in dark theme after a read-only check, with Settings and About buttons at the top. Five task cards each have a switch turned on, drawn with a bar to show it is on: System packages (12 available), Flatpak apps (3 available), Firmware (up to date), Leftover packages and Package cache. Below are a Run selected updates button and a Check for updates button, the message '15 update(s) available — turn on what you want and hit Run.', a log listing the counts per task, and the last run's date and result.
The same OneUp window and check result in light theme, showing it follows the desktop's light or dark setting: identical task cards with their switches on, buttons and log on a white background.

OneUp's Settings window in dark theme, headed 'Background behaviours. Each is off until you turn it on.' Eight rows each explain an option beside its button: Weekly check (on), Passwordless (off), Automatic updates (off, and it needs the passwordless setting), Tray icon (off), Start at boot (off), Copy diagnostics, Text size (Normal) and High contrast (off).

video.caption: A 40-second trailer for OneUp, with background music and soft clicks but no speech; everything it says is written on screen. It is styled like a computer terminal: green and white monospaced lettering over a dark background of faint scrolling text. It opens with "Updating openSUSE is five chores. Easy to forget one.", then the OneUp logo and "Every openSUSE update, one click". Four clips of the app follow, each with a caption below. OneUp's window lists five jobs, each with an on-off switch: System packages, Flatpak apps, Firmware, Leftover packages and Package cache. "See what needs updating": Check for updates is clicked, and System packages shows 24 available while Flatpak apps and Firmware show up to date. "Every package, old and new version": System packages opens into a list of package names, each with its current version, an arrow and its new version. "Pick which jobs to run": the Firmware and Leftover packages switches are turned off. "One click updates everything": Run selected updates is clicked, and a progress bar shows the 24 packages downloading and then installing, while System packages and Flatpak apps change to Done. Three lines follow: "System, Flatpak and firmware updates", "Clears leftovers and old downloads" and "Roll back in one click". Then "openSUSE Tumbleweed · Leap" and "Install with zypper, or run the AppImage". It ends on the logo with "Free and fully open source", "Download it free at antsprojectshub.co.za", and links to support the project on GitHub Sponsors, Patreon and Paybru. The updates shown are a replay of a real update with personal details removed.

projects.name: Groundwork
projects.tagline: Sets up a fresh openSUSE install the way you want, in one sitting.
projects.blurb: Groundwork checks the computer first, then offers choices level by level: essentials (system updates, media codecs, Flatpak and Flathub, and drivers only where your hardware needs them), system setup (snapshots, firewall, firmware updates, laptop power), configuration (computer name, remote login, the clock for dual-boot) and extras (popular apps, gaming, developer tools, a backup tool, fonts). Nothing changes until you press Apply, and it asks for your password once. It also looks after the computer afterwards: it keeps the desktop responsive when memory runs out, offers a safe keyboard restart for a frozen machine, and starts sooner. A single AppImage for Tumbleweed, Slowroll and Leap 16.

screenshots.alt: Groundwork's Essentials page in its dark theme, headed 'What a desktop needs for things to work.' Each item checks itself first, and says what it found. Each row has an on/off switch, what it found and a plain description. 'Bring the system up to date' says no updates were waiting. Media codecs, Flatpak and Flathub, and Video acceleration on AMD graphics say 'already done'. The NVIDIA graphics driver, Sound firmware and Broadcom Wi-Fi rows are greyed out and say 'not needed here', each with the reason, such as 'No NVIDIA graphics card was found.'

Groundwork's Nice to have page, headed 'Extras. Each one is its own choice.' A list of apps, each with a tick box, a status and a one-line description: Google Chrome, Brave, VLC, Discord, Spotify, Steam and Build tools say 'already done'; Zoom and Bottles are ticked and say 'not done'; VSCodium is not done and not ticked.

Groundwork's Ready to apply page, headed 'These run in this order after one password.' It lists three jobs with what each does: bring the system up to date, install Zoom, and install Bottles. Back, Apply and Cancel buttons sit at the bottom.

Groundwork's welcome page: 'Groundwork sets up this computer the way you want. Each page offers a level of choices, from essentials to extras. Nothing changes until you press Apply.' A language menu is set to English, and the line 'Checking this computer…' shows it is looking at the machine before offering anything.

The Groundwork logo follows, with the line 'Set up openSUSE in one window'. projects.name: LottoTracker
projects.tagline: Catches the lottery win sitting unnoticed in your inbox.
projects.blurb: Reads the lottery ticket confirmations your bank sends by SMS, remembers every ticket, and checks them against the real draw results — so a small win doesn't sit unnoticed until it expires. It works out every draw you paid to enter, scores each line, prices the wins, and flags what is still claimable and when it runs out. Everything stays on your own machine: no account, no API key, nothing paid. Specific to the South African National Lottery and, for now, Standard Bank's SMS wording.

screenshots.alt: Lotto Tracker's dark page, using invented tickets. Below a notice that one of seven entries cannot be checked, a Not yet paid section lists one win: the ticket's numbers beside the numbers drawn as coloured balls, Division 9, R15.00, marked unpaid, and the date it expires, 345 days away. Below that, Still outstanding lists the tickets with draws to come and the one entry that cannot be checked, because no results source publishes its pool.
A table of every ticket entry with its cost, how many draws were checked and what it won, followed by money spent against money won for the year.

Totals comparing what was spent with what was won, then the settings: a colour theme choice, switches for starting the tray at login and opening this page when the tray starts, and a Refresh results button.

projects.name: demoreel
projects.tagline: Record an app's demo video without filming your desktop.
projects.blurb: Records a short video of a desktop app running on a private virtual display — so nothing else you have open, and none of your accessibility tools, ends up in a file destined for a public pull request. One command takes an app and hands back a video file, optionally running a scripted list of clicks and keystrokes so the recording shows the app being used rather than sitting still. It refuses to return a blank recording: an empty display is an error, not a video.

screenshots.alt: A terminal running demoreel record on the GTK demo app for six seconds; demoreel prints two status lines, then the path of the finished video
A frame from that video: the GTK Demo app filling the whole picture, with no desktop, panel or other windows
A still taken with --gpu: the Vulkan test cube, textured with the LunarG logo, drawn by the graphics card, which the default virtual display cannot do

video.caption: A 47-second trailer for demoreel, with music, in a dark green terminal style. It opens on two lines: 'You need an app video. Your whole desktop gets filmed.' The demoreel logo follows, with the line 'Record any app, never your desktop'. A terminal runs 'demoreel record -o calc.mp4 -d 3 --app-log app.log -- kcalc'; demoreel says it is recording, then prints the finished file's path. Caption: 'One command records any app'. KDE's calculator, filling the whole picture, has 4, 5, ×, 1, 2 and = clicked in turn by demoreel. Caption: 'It clicks and types for you'. The same sum plays in a rounded window with a soft shadow, over a slowly moving coloured background. Caption: 'A framed window, ready to share'. A smooth zoom closes in on the answer, 540. Caption: 'Zoom in on what matters'. The demoreel logo grows into view, and 'Record any app' and 'and make it a film' slide up beneath it. Caption: 'Titles that slide into place'. One calculator scene slides away to the next. Caption: 'Smooth changes between scenes'. Three lines follow: 'Your desktop never appears', 'Trim, caption and join clips' and 'Add music and sounds'. Then 'Linux', above 'openSUSE · Debian · Ubuntu · Fedora · Arch'. It ends on the logo with 'Free and fully open source', 'Download it free at antsprojectshub.co.za', and links to GitHub Sponsors, Patreon and Paybru. demoreel recorded and edited every calculator scene itself.

projects.name: Local Web Server Manager
projects.tagline: See which of your local web servers are actually running.
projects.blurb: If you keep several web projects in one folder, each starts a different way, on a different port, and nothing tells you which are running. This scans your projects folder, works out how each one starts and which port it wants, and gives you a window with a row per project: a status light, a Start/Stop button and a link to open it. It runs each project's own start script and never edits your projects. Early days, but it runs: the window opens, the lights are live, and Start, Stop, Restart and Open work — driven from the keyboard if you prefer, with eight colour themes including two high-contrast ones. Its first release is the source code only, so for now you run it from that; a packaged download is planned.

screenshots.alt: The Local Web Server Manager window in its dark Midnight theme, listing five sample web projects: Photo Gallery and Book Club are running, shown with green dots, Recipe Box and Budget Planner are stopped, and Weather Dashboard is unknown because it has no port. Each row has its port, a browser picker and Start, Stop, Restart and Open buttons.
The same five sample projects in the light Ledger theme, dark text on warm off-white, with the two running projects' Stop, Restart and Open buttons enabled.
The project list in the High contrast dark theme, white text with bright green and yellow status words on pure black, for readers who need the strongest contrast.
The word "book" typed into the filter box at the top narrows the list to the one matching project, Book Club, running on port 8604.

projects.name: Pressless
projects.tagline: Write and publish your own website from your own computer.
projects.blurb: A writing app that runs on your own machine and opens in your normal browser: you type an entry, see it exactly as it will look, and click once to publish it to your own free website — GitHub Pages today, with other hosts likely to follow. No accounts, no monthly fee and no service in between — every entry stays an ordinary text file in an ordinary folder, readable with Pressless closed, deleted or never installed. It is deliberately not a host: it never talks to your visitors and is not reachable from the internet. Writing, previewing, publishing, undo, photographs and a visitor dashboard work today; running the whole site is still to come.

screenshots.alt: Writing an entry in Pressless: the title, categories, tags and address on the left above the writing box, the finished page shown live on the right, with Press to site, Undo the last press and Add a photograph buttons
The same entry in Pressless's dark look, with the preview dimmed so the bright page does not glare, and a tick box above it to show the preview in its true colours

The list in the high-contrast light look, chosen from the Theme picker in the top bar: black text and outlines on white

Editing the site's Home page on the page itself: the finished page on the right, with its paragraph picked and a Drag handle beside it, and on the left the tools for that section: Bold, Italic, Link, add a section below it, move it up or down, or remove it

Setup's Sign in to GitHub page: four numbered steps (press Next, open the link and type the code on GitHub, click Authorize, come back and press Next again), a short code to type, the GitHub address to type it at, and a Next button
